summary: The rebuilt linkage counts, rates, sample restrictions, contradicted-share arithmetic, and slide rounding agree with the new tables and code. The principal remaining problem is interpretive: the headline 28 percent “match quality” improvement compares old and new links using different 1940 middle-initial validators, so it does not measure a pure change in link quality. Panel B also labels only net entries and exits from linkage as added and removed pairs, omitting changed partners.

findings.title: The headline 28 percent match-quality improvement switches the validating transcription between old and new links
findings.what_the_code_does: For old links the code sets `miv` to `mi_anc`, while for new links it sets `miv` to `mi_ml`, then computes `count if mi1930 == mi1940`. Thus the reported 65.4-to-83.6 percent comparison changes both the linked pairs and the 1940 value used to validate them. The repository's fixed-validator diagnostic shows that the 18.2 percentage-point own-initial rise decomposes into only 10.3 points when Ancestry's initial is held fixed, or 8.4 points when FamilySearch's is held fixed; the remaining 7.9 or 9.8 points arise from changing the transcription of the validator itself.
findings.why_it_matters: The abstract and introduction describe the full 28 percent relative rise as improved “match quality,” although roughly half of the percentage-point increase is mechanically due to rescoring links against the model's own different reading of the middle initial. The body discloses this decomposition, but the headline claim still overstates the independently measured improvement in link quality.
findings.how_to_check: Run `replication/diagnostics/validation_fixed_initials.do` and inspect `replication/results/validation_fixed_initials.tex`, especially `ppTotalTarget`, `ppLinksAncTarget`, `ppReadingAncTarget`, `ppLinksFsTarget`, and `ppReadingFsTarget`. Compare those results with the 65.4 and 83.6 percent headline rates.
findings.suggested_fix: State the fixed-validator result in the abstract and introduction as the link-quality estimate, identifying which fixed source is used. Retain the 65.4-to-83.6 comparison only under an explicit label such as “own-transcription middle-initial agreement,” separate from link quality.

findings.title: Panel B calls net linkage entries and exits added and removed pairs while omitting partner changes
findings.what_the_code_does: The code classifies a 1930 person linked in both versions to different 1940 partners as `status = "changed"`. It then builds the displayed Added rows only from `status == "net_added"` and Removed rows only from `status == "net_removed"`; changed links are calculated separately but never written to Panel B. The paper note instead says Panel B “decomposes the pairs added and removed when moving from the old transcription to the new,” even though a changed partner entails one removed pair and one added pair that the panel excludes.
findings.why_it_matters: Panel B understates total pair turnover and does not describe the composition of all pairs added and removed. Its displayed added-minus-removed category counts therefore need not reconcile the changes in Panel A, potentially misleading readers who interpret it as a complete pair-level decomposition.
findings.how_to_check: After the `tab status` commands, tabulate `status` for each method and sample and compare the number of `changed` observations with the displayed Panel B totals. Reconcile `new pairs - old pairs` both with and without treating each changed observation as one added and one removed pair.
findings.suggested_fix: Either relabel Panel B and its note as a decomposition of 1930 persons newly linked versus no longer linked, explicitly excluding partner switches, or include changed partners as one removed old pair and one added new pair and regenerate the category totals.

review_limits: The external census, linkage, and truth datasets were not readable in this sandbox, so counts could not be independently recomputed and the Stata pipeline was not rerun.
The review verified source logic, committed generated tables, diagnostic outputs, and paper arithmetic; runtime assertions and the recorded one-to-one data check were not independently repeated.
The construction and substantive accuracy of the selected FamilySearch genealogical reference links could not be validated from the underlying profiles or images.
The third-party HLINK matching run itself is outside this repository; only its imported pair files and downstream scoring code were reviewable.
